text: A young man is sent to Germany to have his damaged eyes treated, and finds his sister living there, married to a German. Ebrahim Hatamikia gives himself ninety-two minutes and mostly one problem: two people raised in the same house who now hold no country in common and no agreement about what the fighting was for. The Iran-Iraq War is never staged. It arrives as damage already done, carried through customs inside a passenger's body, and Leyla's marriage becomes the film's real dispute - a life built elsewhere, examined by a brother who paid for staying in a way she did not. It took the Crystal Simorgh for Best Film. Around Saeed's surgery the picture simply holds: a bright foreign room, an appointment ahead of him, a sister across the table with a life he has no way to read.

The confession here is performed rather than whispered: prisoners in costume, a stage improvised inside a prison, and one listener who is not free to leave. In 1952 Bishop Bilodeau arrives to hear Simon, jailed forty years for murder, and what he gets is a play about the boyhood the two of them shared. John Greyson keeps the audience of one inside the frame, so every scene is being received as well as acted, and the room's power runs backwards for once - the man with nothing left decides what gets told, the man with a title has to sit still for it. The Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television gave it Best Motion Picture. Ninety-six minutes, two eras loaded onto the same stage, and a church discovering it was summoned rather than consulted.

These friends met online, which puts them outside the arrangements - family, neighbourhood, school - that usually decide who knows whom. Abolhassan Davoodi hands them a game: a bet taken up lightly, with a floor much further down than anyone bothered to measure. Ninety minutes is a tight frame for it, and the crime is less an event than an accounting, each of them working out afterwards which part of the thing was his. The premise sounds like a stunt. The design is not - the wager exists to make a group of young people say out loud what they actually believe about money, luck and one another, which is a harder scene to write than the dare that sets it going. Davoodi's film left with the Crystal Simorgh for Best Film.

Tsatsiki has a mother in a rock band, a lodger with a police motorcycle, and a father he has never met, described to him as a fisherman in Greece. Ella Lemhagen films the household at the boy's height, which is exactly where the matchmaking makes sense: the policeman is orderly and nearby, the mother is neither, and the bass player she actually wants is an obstacle to be worked around. The script keeps her own appetites in frame rather than tidying them offscreen, which is what gives the boy's campaign its friction - he is not filling a vacancy, he is competing. A Guldbagge for Best Film followed. Ninety-one minutes, and the plan is neither cute nor correct, which is the most respectful thing a family picture can do with a child's logic.

The Greek tragedy's argument - family against the law - moves whole into present-day Montreal, conducted in French by people whose place in the country is provisional. Sophie Deraspe keeps the structure and changes what does the enforcing: not a ruler who can be defied to his face, but hearings, files and officials following procedure. That exchange is the whole idea. A refusal that once cost a single household everything now runs into a system built to absorb refusals, and the woman making it has to keep insisting in person, in rooms designed to outlast her. The Toronto International Film Festival named it the best Canadian film of its year. At 109 minutes nothing is hurried, which is how the tragedy's clock is rebuilt: each step arrives on time and cannot be talked out of arriving.

A mine left in the ground after a war has ended still belongs to that war. Ebrahim Hatamikia builds ninety-six minutes on that fact: a daughter injured by ordnance from the Iran-Iraq conflict, and a father who has to hold what the fighting was said to be for against what it has done to her. The split is generational, and it is the entire design - she chose none of it and inherits it anyway, while his vocabulary for it has stopped explaining anything. Made in 2005, at a distance from the front the daughter's body does not share. Nothing is set on a battlefield. The pressure is domestic and unrelieved - two people in rooms, one injury that will not be reasoned with, one man's certainty asked to account for itself.

On 9 April 1940 the German army entered Norway, and the country's most admired living novelist welcomed it. Jan Troell takes 159 minutes over that, about the right length for a case that will not close in a sentence. Knut Hamsun's hatred of the English was old and personal - he blamed them for the hunger Norway went through in the earlier war - and it made occupation look like protection. Then the arrests started, and the executions, and he objected to those while keeping the ideas underneath them. Marie travels in Germany as the visible half of the couple's loyalty; the marriage and the politics wear each other down at the same rate. Troell's patience is the method. A man is wrong at length, at his own speed, in his own house, and the film declines to shorten the process.

In a remote Costa Rican village, a household has arranged itself around a forty-year-old woman who is not expected to want anything for herself. Clara's awakening, when it comes, is bodily and religious at once, and Nathalie Álvarez Mesén refuses to separate the two, which is what turns the piety around her into a fence rather than a comfort. The listing says fantasy. What that means in practice is that her inner life is given the same standing as the village's rules - not explained, not diagnosed, simply there and inconvenient. A Guldbagge for Best Director went to Álvarez Mesén, and direction is where the film lives: 106 minutes spent watching a woman's attention move toward things nobody has given her permission to notice.

Two singers in a community choir want to be left alone together, and everyone who loves them treats that as a problem to be managed. Gabrielle has Williams syndrome and a gift for music; Martin sings beside her; the recreation centre that introduced them is also where the relationship is most closely watched. Louise Archambault keeps the practical questions in view - where a person is allowed to live, who decides, what independence costs in small daily arrangements - instead of settling for a lesson about difference. The choir's festival supplies the clock. The fear around the couple is not stupid or cruel; it comes from people who love them and have made themselves responsible, which is the harder version of the obstacle and the one Archambault insists on.

A handful of days, a crowded house on the edge of Rio de Janeiro, and a mother who has to be ready by the time they run out. Irene's eldest son is leaving; Gustavo Pizzi films the interval before that, which is a stranger subject than the departure itself. Everything happens at kitchen level. The outskirts here are a working address, not scenery. The household keeps running, other people keep needing things, and the ninety-five minutes fill with interruptions that have no interest in her deadline, so the anxiety never gets a scene of its own - it is distributed through chores, arguments and the arithmetic of a house with too many people in it. IFFR's audience award fits it: the film asks to be recognised rather than admired.

Assassination, in a film shaped like this one, is mostly a logistics problem: distance, timing, who can safely be told a name. By 1909 Korea has been a Japanese colony for several years, and the answer a small group of independence fighters arrives at is one man, one plan and a long way to travel. Woo Min-ho works in thriller grammar - surveillance, borders, the slow attrition of a scheme carried by people who can be followed - and since the history is settled, the suspense has to come from the waiting rather than the outcome. It was named best film at the Baeksang Arts Awards. At 108 minutes the action is there, but the subject is the cost of keeping a conspiracy alive among people who have already lost the country they are fighting for.

One brother comes back to Quebec to bury his father; the other, adopted, is trying to find out whose son he is. The question turns out to be older than both of them, and Robert Lepage runs the present alongside the Quebec of the 1950s until the two are moving on one track, so that a search through records becomes a suspense structure rather than a family errand. The mystery label is earned by method. Information is withheld the way a province withholds it - in registries, in what was agreed not to be said, in the distance between an official record and a household's account of itself. A hundred minutes, in French, and Lepage is finally less interested in settling Marc's parentage than in the arrangement that made the answer worth hiding.
